title: planqc Expands Into the UK With New Cambridge Site
html:
Insider Brief

  • German quantum computing company planqc is expanding into the United Kingdom with a new subsidiary and a neutral-atom quantum computing site in Cambridge.
  • The Cambridge site will house a laboratory to assemble, integrate and test quantum computers, with planqc aiming to build a team of about 20 people.
  • planqc will work with the University of Cambridge’s Cavendish Laboratory to develop optical lattices, which use laser light to arrange atoms and could help scale quantum processors.

PRESS RELEASE — planqc, one of Europe’s leading developers of neutral-atom quantum computers, is expanding into the United Kingdom with the establishment of planqc UK Ltd and a new site in Cambridge. The company is investing in the double-digit millions in the UK.

Cambridge will host a full neutral-atom laboratory for the assembly, integration and commissioning of quantum computing systems, including laser and optical subsystems, with the aim of delivering systems from the UK. planqc is building a team of specialists in Cambridge over the next two years: quantum hardware engineers, error-correction and system-integration engineers, software and FPGA engineers, plus site management and back-office support. Several of these roles are already filled by colleagues transferring from Munich and Cambridge. The company’s medium-term ambition for the site is in the order of 20 people.

In collaboration with Professor Ulrich Schneider’s group at the University of Cambridge’s Cavendish Laboratory, planqc will develop next-generation optical lattice technology. Alongside its Germany headquarters in Garching, Cambridge will become another centre where planqc works with academic and industry partners to advance neutral-atom quantum computing.

planqc employs more than 130 people and has raised €55 million in seed and Series A financing, alongside major publicly funded quantum computing projects, including the €29 million DiNAQC contract and the €19.1 million MAQCS consortium project. Together, these announced financing and project volumes exceed €100 million. The expansion is also supported by Hermann Hauser, co-founder of ARM and Amadeus Capital Partners. Hauser has been an investor and advisory board member of planqc since 2023 and has played a defining role in Cambridge’s technology ecosystem for almost five decades.

“With ARM, we demonstrated in Cambridge that superior architecture ultimately wins out. I believe quantum computing will be no different, and neutral atoms in optical lattices are among the approaches I see as having the greatest potential. The fact that planqc is now advancing this architecture at the Cavendish Laboratory, where I completed my own PhD, brings things full circle for me. Europe has an opportunity not just to use the next major computing platform, but to help shape it,” says Hermann Hauser, co-founder of ARM and Amadeus Capital Partners and Honorary Fellow of King’s College, Cambridge.

The UK as a Quantum Computing Hub:

Following the opening of its subsidiary in Innsbruck, Cambridge will be planqc’s second location outside Germany. The new site will give the company a foothold in the UK market and extend its research network beyond Germany and Austria. In Germany, planqc is building quantum computers for the German Aerospace Center (DLR) and the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre (LRZ), while developing early applications with partners including Airbus, the European Space Agency (ESA) and Fraunhofer institutes, supported by its team in Innsbruck. planqc intends to bring this close integration of hardware development, research and applications to the UK.

planqc’s research roots lie at the Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics and LMU Munich. The new Cambridge site will extend this network to leading British universities, starting with the University of Cambridge’s Cavendish Laboratory. On the applications side, planqc will focus particularly on UK industries with substantial computing requirements. These include financial services, with London ranking among the world’s largest financial centres, and the pharmaceutical and life sciences sectors, which have a major hub in Cambridge. In the future, quantum computers are expected to tackle problems in these fields that are beyond the reach of classical computers, such as simulating molecules for new drug development or performing complex optimisation and risk calculations.

The expansion into the UK also forms part of planqc’s broader European strategy. Europe is among the world’s leading regions for neutral atom quantum computing, and planqc develops and manufactures its systems using European suppliers specialising in laser, photonics and vacuum technologies. With sites in Germany, Austria and now the UK, the company is bringing together expertise from several major European quantum technology clusters to maintain and strengthen this position.

“The UK has one of the strongest quantum ecosystems in the world, combining outstanding universities, a growing industry and investors with a long-term commitment to deep tech. With planqc UK, we are becoming part of that ecosystem. In Cambridge, we are building expertise across the entire technology stack, from hardware development to software and applications, while working closely with our teams in Garching and Innsbruck. Together with partners from industry and academia, we are establishing another centre of expertise in neutral atom quantum computing,” says Dr Benedikt Battke, Head of Corporate Development at planqc.

Optical Lattices: A Key to Scaling Quantum Computers:

planqc uses individual neutral atoms as qubits. These are trapped and controlled in optical tweezer arrays comprising thousands of trapping sites. This technology is complemented by optical lattices: Overlapping laser beams create a periodic light pattern with potentially millions of identical trapping sites that can be filled with atoms. This architecture provides an essential foundation for scaling quantum processors to large numbers of qubits and is precisely the field of research in which Prof. Ulrich Schneider’s group at the Cavendish Laboratory is internationally recognised.

“Neutral atoms in optical lattices offer the fastest and most scalable platform for quantum computing. We are taking the next step together with Ulrich Schneider and his group, one of the world’s leading teams in the field of atoms in optical lattices. In Cambridge, we will combine their expertise with our hardware capabilities to develop quantum processing units that can scale to millions of qubits,” says Dr Sebastian Blatt, CTO and co-founder of planqc.

The group investigates the behaviour and control of ultracold atoms in optical lattices, including non-periodic structures such as optical quasicrystals. Schneider was awarded the Institute of Physics’ Joseph Thomson Medal in 2023. Before moving to Cambridge in 2015, he led a research group at LMU Munich, the same academic environment from which planqc emerged in 2022.

“Optical lattices allow us to arrange atoms in a wide variety of geometries and control them with great precision. Together with planqc, we are applying this knowledge to lattice architectures for larger and more powerful quantum processors. For my group, this is an opportunity to translate fundamental research directly into technology,” says Professor Ulrich Schneider, Professor of Many-Body Physics at the University of Cambridge’s Cavendish Laboratory.

Building the Cambridge Team:

The UK subsidiary will be led by planqc co-founder Dr Sebastian Blatt, who will take on this responsibility alongside his existing role as CTO of planqc. An experimental physicist, Blatt spent around a decade conducting research at Harvard University and the University of Colorado before establishing his own research group at the Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics in 2015 and subsequently at LMU Munich. He is known for his work on the world’s most precise atomic clocks, which are also based on atoms held in optical lattices. The Cambridge team is expected to grow steadily over the coming years.
